title: Loss of persistence of early growth advantages in chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus)
content:
Abstract
The growth–survival paradigm (GSP) predicts that faster early growth enhances survival to recruitment, yet clear support is found in only about half of published studies. Although the GSP links early growth to recruitment, empirical studies have focused primarily on the larval stage, leaving the persistence of early growth advantages until recruitment poorly understood. Here, we examine the consequences of early growth for later size and growth in chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) using field-collected and laboratory-reared samples. Daily otolith increment analyses of wild-caught adults revealed consistent negative relationships between larval growth rates and adult body size across year classes and sexes, with adult size most strongly associated with growth up to the 10th daily increment. A rearing experiment under ad libitum feeding and constant conditions showed a significant negative correlation between larval- and late-juvenile growth rates, resulting in a convergence in body size such that early growth was no longer associated with body size at approximately 150 mm standard length. Together, these results suggest that the negative association between early growth and adult size in wild chub mackerel can be explained, at least in part, by intrinsic changes in relative growth rates among individuals during the late juvenile stage. Such changes may alter relative size among individuals before recruitment, thereby offsetting the expected advantages of rapid early growth. This perspective suggests a mechanism by which the relationship between early growth and survival to recruitment may be modified, potentially contributing to cases in which the GSP does not hold.
